tldr: We propose "LyEvO", a framework that uses a safety region derived from Lyapunov stability analysis as a starting point, combining Evolutionary Strategies and Statistical Model Checking to jointly optimize policies and expand their safe operational regions. It demonstrates robust zero-shot sim-to-real transfer under disturbances not only in simulation, but also on physical cartpole and quadrotor platforms.
hero_caption: On a cartpole, the candidate stability region obtained from initial linear analysis (solid ellipse) is significantly expanded by LyEvO up to the boundaries of the safety constraints (dashed square), forming the expanded region (dashed ellipse). While preserving the geometric shape of the Lyapunov function, the region where safety is statistically certified is pushed outward in stages.
overview:
Sim-to-Real—training learning-based controllers such as reinforcement learning in simulation and directly deploying them to physical hardware—is a powerful methodology. Yet, the persistent worry remains: "Will it actually operate safely in the real world?" While conventional safe RL and robust RL excel at improving average performance, formally guaranteeing the operational envelope—specifically, knowing for which range of initial states and disturbances the system is provably safe—has remained extremely difficult.

To tackle this, the authors devised "LyEvO", an approach that fuses classical control theory insights with modern formal verification techniques. First, using the direct Lyapunov method on linearized robot dynamics, they compute a small, guaranteed-stable "initial candidate stability region". Next, operational scenarios consisting of initial states and disturbance sequences are sampled from within this region, followed by an iterative loop that alternates between policy optimization via Evolutionary Strategies (ES) and safety/performance bound verification via Statistical Model Checking (SMC). Once verification passes, the region is expanded slightly along its principal axes, and the cycle of learning and verification repeats.

The framework was evaluated on two benchmarks: a cartpole (inverted pendulum) and a 3D quadrotor. In simulation, while all conventional safe RL baselines failed statistical verification, LyEvO successfully passed rigorous verification with less than a 1% constraint violation probability, achieving stability regions up to 224 times larger. Furthermore, in physical hardware experiments subjected to strong wind disturbances, the verified policies demonstrated smooth, stable trajectory tracking without crashing, outperforming the baselines.
contributions: Formulated LyEvO, a control synthesis framework that organically integrates linear Lyapunov analysis, constrained Evolutionary Strategies, and Statistical Model Checking (SMC)
Established a framework to formally verify, with statistical confidence, the satisfaction of safety constraints and a guaranteed minimum return for any scenario within an expanded stability region
Expanded the theoretically provable stability regions by 6.14x for the cartpole and 224.04x for the quadrotor over baseline analytical methods
Demonstrated successful real-world transfer on physical cartpole and quadrotor platforms under strong wind disturbances, with verified policies exhibiting superior robustness compared to baselines

sections.heading: How can we build policies that deploy safely to physical hardware?
sections.summary: This section discusses the necessity of a new framework that simultaneously provides formal safety guarantees and identifies the safe operational envelope to bridge the Sim-to-Real gap. Using classical Lyapunov stability regions as a guide for evolutionary optimization forms the starting point of this paper.
sections.details:
Training control policies in simulation has achieved remarkable success in robotics. However, deploying them in the physical world—where modeling errors and unknown disturbances exist—carries substantial risks of unexpected constraint violations and catastrophic failures. This is the well-known Sim-to-Real gap.

Existing safe RL and robust RL approaches attempt to boost robustness by penalizing cost functions or optimizing for worst-case outcomes. Yet, after training completes, they cannot provide formal guarantees defining the precise range of initial states and disturbances over which the policy remains safe. Conversely, post-hoc formal verification and counterexample generation techniques exist, but because they are disconnected from the training loop, it is difficult to remediate policies when verification fails.

"LyEvO" resolves this disconnect by placing physics-grounded Lyapunov stability analysis in the driver's seat of the optimization loop. Anchored by an analytically derived initial stability region, it couples counterexample-guided evolutionary strategies with Statistical Model Checking (SMC) to refine the policy while gradually expanding the boundary of the statistically certified safe region outward. Consequently, before hardware deployment, operators obtain a certified policy and operational region accompanied by explicit guarantees: with confidence at least $1-\delta$, the probability of constraint violation or performance drop is at most $\varepsilon$.

sections.heading: From Markov Decision Processes to Evolutionary Strategies and Statistical Model Checking
sections.summary: This section formulates discrete-time dynamics under disturbance as an MDP, comparing Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) with black-box Evolutionary Strategies (ES). It also explains the mechanics of "SMC-ES", a prior verification-driven algorithm.
sections.details:
The problem setting considers a discrete-time dynamical system $s_{t+1} = f(s_t, a_t, w_t)$ subjected to unknown disturbances $w_t \in \mathcal{W}$. A pair consisting of an initial state $s_0$ chosen from a candidate region $\Omega$ and a disturbance sequence drawn from a stochastic process is defined as an "operational scenario". The system must strictly satisfy hard constraint functions $c_i(s_t, a_t, s_{t+1}) \leq 0$.

For policy search, the paper contrasts two primary approaches:
- **Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)**: Typically uses Actor-Critic architectures that learn policies and value functions simultaneously. In safe RL, constraints are handled via techniques like Lagrangian relaxation; however, because they rely on expectation optimization, they cannot completely eliminate rare, catastrophic failure scenarios.
- **Evolutionary Strategies (ES)**: A black-box optimization method that avoids backpropagating gradients directly. Instead, it perturbs policy parameters randomly across multiple candidates, evaluates them in parallel, and estimates update directions from fitness score differences. It has the distinct advantage of directly optimizing undiscounted cumulative rewards and constraint violations over a finite horizon $H$.

For formal verification, the authors adopt their previously proposed "SMC-ES" as a subroutine. This loop alternates between optimizing policies with ES and testing them against large numbers of sampled scenarios via Statistical Model Checking (SMC). If a counterexample violating constraints is found, it is permanently added to the training set for retraining. This yields a solution pair $(\pi^*, \beta^*)$—where $\beta^*$ is a guaranteed minimum return—backed by statistical guarantees defined by an allowable failure probability $\varepsilon$ and a confidence level $1-\delta$.

sections.heading: Expanding operational envelopes guided by Lyapunov stability analysis
sections.summary: By solving a Linear Matrix Inequality (LMI) derived from linear prior dynamics, an initial ellipsoidal stability region is computed and formulated into a bi-level optimization problem that pushes its boundaries toward safety limits. Geometric expansion and robust control are elegantly united.
sections.details:
In robotics, "safety" can often be framed as maximizing the Region of Attraction (ROA)—the set of states from which the system can reliably return and converge to the target state. However, analytically computing the true ROA for high-dimensional nonlinear systems is impossible.

Therefore, this method decomposes the dynamics into a linear part and a nonlinear residual, applying the direct Lyapunov method to the nominal linear closed-loop system. By solving a convex optimization problem under Linear Matrix Inequalities (LMIs) enforcing state and input constraints, it analytically computes a quadratic Lyapunov function $V(s) = s^\top P s$ and linear gain $F$, establishing a provably invariant and stable initial ellipsoidal candidate region $\Omega = \{s \mid s^\top P s \leq 1\}$.

Here lies the core innovation of LyEvO. An eigendecomposition of the matrix $P = U \Lambda U^\top$ reveals that the eigenvectors $U$ define the principal axis directions of the ellipsoid, while the eigenvalues $1/\sqrt{\lambda_i}$ determine the semi-axis lengths. Preserving this geometric orientation, the ellipsoid is scaled using expansion factors $\gamma_i$ to define an expanded region $\Omega_\gamma = \{s \mid s^\top P_\gamma s \leq 1\}$.

The overall formulation is cast as a bi-level optimization problem. The outer loop maximizes the volume of the ellipsoid (minimizing $\sum \log \gamma_i$), while the inner loop searches for a policy $\pi_\theta$ that achieves zero constraint violations and maximizes the worst-case cumulative reward $\beta$ across all scenarios within the expanded region. To prevent the ellipsoid from violating physical limits (such as position and velocity boundaries), the expansion limit along each axis, $\gamma_{\min,i}$, is precomputed analytically.

The inner solid line represents the initial candidate region obtained from the LMI, while the outer dashed line shows the expanded region pushed by LyEvO to the boundaries of the safety constraints (red dashed lines). Scatter points indicate the Lyapunov values of sampled scenarios.

sections.heading: Outer loop expands the region, inner loop runs evolutionary search and formal verification
sections.summary: To tractably solve the bi-level optimization problem, a practical algorithm was designed consisting of an outer loop that greedily expands the region dimension-by-dimension, and an inner loop that updates policies, learns from counterexamples, and performs formal verification using SMC-ES.
sections.details:
Searching globally and rigorously for the exact solution to the bi-level problem is computationally intractable (even inner worst-case maximization alone is undecidable). LyEvO addresses this through a smart, greedy heuristic.

First, with the scaling vector initialized to $\gamma = \mathbf{1}$ over the initial region $\Omega$, the algorithm executes the $\text{SMC-ES}$ subroutine to synthesize an initial policy that satisfies statistical guarantees. Upon success, it enters the outer loop, greedily selecting one principal axis with expansion headroom at a time and decreasing $\gamma_i$ (expanding the ellipsoid) by a fixed step size.

At each expansion step, new scenarios are uniformly sampled from the newly defined region $\Omega_\gamma$, and the inner-loop $\text{SMC-ES}$ is restarted. Within this subroutine, evolutionary optimization alternates with formal SMC verification. Whenever a scenario violates constraints or falls below the target return (a counterexample), it is immediately added to the training set, forcing the policy to adapt.

The algorithm terminates when no axis can be expanded further without failing verification or when a maximum iteration limit is reached. The final output is a tuple containing the maximized stability region $\Omega^*_\gamma$, the optimized policy $\pi_{\theta^*}$, and the guaranteed return $\beta^*$. This issues a rigorous statistical certificate: with confidence $1-\delta$, the probability of policy failure within the expanded region is at most $\varepsilon$.

sections.heading: Massive region expansion in simulation and strong wind resilience on real hardware
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted on a 4-DoF cartpole and a 12-DoF quadrotor. In simulation, DRL baselines uniformly failed formal verification while LyEvO achieved up to a 224x region expansion. Real-world experiments using industrial fans confirmed superior stability and tracking accuracy.
sections.details:
The experiments rigorously evaluated the framework across both simulation and physical hardware.

**1. Implementation and Baseline Setup**
The target systems were a 4-dimensional state cartpole and a 12-dimensional state quadrotor directly controlling four rotor thrusts. Evaluated baselines included a Residual policy correcting an LMI controller with RL, standard SAC, SAC-Lyapunov incorporating Lyapunov reward shaping, and constrained SAC-Lagrangian. Additionally, a robust variant, "LyEvO-R", was trained by injecting 5% multiplicative noise into observations and 1% additive noise into actions. Distributed simulations were parallelized on an HPC cluster utilizing up to 1,000 CPU cores.

**2. Simulation Verification Results**
When subjected to Statistical Model Checking (acceptable failure rate $\varepsilon=1\%$, confidence $1-\delta=99\%$), all SAC-based baselines failed verification completely. Because they handle constraints via soft penalties, they failed to prevent worst-case failures or overfitted to training distributions, collapsing on unseen initial states.
In contrast, LyEvO proved that its violation probability (VP) remained strictly below $\varepsilon$ across both the nominal and expanded regions. Furthermore, the volume of the identified stability region expanded by 6.14x for the cartpole and an astounding 224.04x for the quadrotor compared to the initial LMI-certified region.

**3. Physical Hardware Experiments**
Hardware deployment was conducted on a Quanser cartpole and an ANT-X quadrotor, comparing only the certified policies: LyEvO, LyEvO-R, and the mathematically guaranteed LMI controller. Severe stress tests were performed using high-output industrial fans.
- **Cartpole**: In recovery tests initialized with cart offsets up to 0.28 m, LyEvO-R achieved the highest cumulative return and the shortest settling time. Under external disturbance, it exhibited the smallest transient oscillations and exceptional stability.
- **Quadrotor**: In a waypoint-tracking mission, the baseline LMI controller could not withstand aerodynamic disturbances and unmodeled dynamics, leading to catastrophic failure (crash). Standard LyEvO was agile but produced slightly aggressive transient actions, whereas noise-trained LyEvO-R outputted sufficiently smooth control commands, achieving the best performance in both mean tracking error and trajectory smoothness.

sections.heading: Remaining challenges in computational overhead and control smoothness
sections.summary: The authors candidly discuss practical trade-offs for real-world adoption, including the lower sample efficiency of evolutionary strategies (long runtimes), tuning the step size for region expansion, and high-frequency actuator jitter observed on physical hardware.
sections.details:
Several practical limitations must be addressed when deploying this framework in real-world scenarios.

First, there is a sample efficiency trade-off. Because Evolutionary Strategies do not utilize backpropagation, they generally require significantly more environment interactions than DRL. This study utilized 1,000 CPU cores in parallel, requiring approximately 31.5 hours to train LyEvO-R on the quadrotor (a substantial computational footprint compared to single-CPU DRL baselines taking ~10 hours).

Second, designing the expansion step size requires care. If the step size is too large, the framework may prematurely fail verification and miss viable expansion directions; if it is too small, iteration counts escalate rapidly. Balancing expansion speed and optimization robustness requires careful tuning.

Third, high-frequency actuator jitter remains an issue. Compared to mathematically smooth LMI controllers, neural network policies inherently tend to induce slight high-frequency chatter in control inputs. Incorporating explicit action smoothness constraints into the objective will be essential in future work.

sections.heading: Fusing control theory and machine learning for verifiable Sim-to-Real transfer
sections.summary: This section reiterates the impact of LyEvO in leveraging physical prior models to progressively certify and expand safety regions, outlining future research directions toward fully nonlinear systems where linear models cannot be constructed.
sections.details:
This work presented "LyEvO", a Sim-to-Real framework unifying physics-based Lyapunov stability analysis, constrained evolutionary optimization, and Statistical Model Checking. By injecting physical knowledge of the robot upfront, the policy search avoids exploring useless areas and focuses on safety-critical scenarios, producing formal statistical evidence of deployment readiness.

Extensive simulations and real-world experiments on both cartpole and quadrotor platforms verified its efficacy. While the current framework assumes linearized dynamics to compute the candidate region, future research aims to extend the approach to arbitrary nonlinear systems without requiring linear approximations, alongside improving overall computational efficiency.

takeaways: Successful training in safe RL does not guarantee safe real-world deployment; integrating formal verification (SMC) provides rigorous, confidence-backed criteria for hardware readiness.
Using a small, analytically certified stability region (e.g., via LMIs) as an initial training anchor and expanding it geometrically is an exceptionally reliable and effective strategy.

Coupling Evolutionary Strategies (ES) with counterexample-guided loops provides remarkable robustness against safety constraints where gradient methods often suffer from vanishing gradients or local minima.

For successful Sim-to-Real transfer, expanding the safety region alone is insufficient; injecting observation and action noise during training (LyEvO-R) smooths control outputs and prevents catastrophic hardware crashes.
limitations: Relying on nominal linear models to derive the initial stability region restricts the initialization procedure when applied to highly nonlinear systems that cannot be linearized.
The computational cost and sample inefficiency inherent to Evolutionary Strategies and iterative verification are substantial, requiring hours to days even on a 1,000-core parallel cluster.
The resulting neural network controllers exhibit more high-frequency actuator chattering (jitter) than analytical linear controllers, raising potential hardware wear concerns.
